synopsis: The rule of three approximates the 95% upper failure-probability bound as 3/n after zero failures; exact one-sided binomial inference uses (1 − q)^n ≤ alpha [f14202, f6875]. At 95% confidence, miss-rate limits of 5%, 1%, 0.1% and 0.01% require respectively 59, 299, 2,995 and 29,956 independent zero-miss trials; at 99% confidence these rise to 90, 459, 4,603 and 46,050 [f14193, f14194]. These counts apply per claimed population, not across an entire product family: separate claims need their own evidence or justified pooling, and 20 critical strata with 1% miss-rate claims require about 6,000 zero-miss trials, described as feasible only in simulation or HIL [f6885, f6886, f14199]. Independence and sampling validity are essential: correlated sensor frames cannot count as separate encounters, and naive binomial intervals from adaptively selected tests are invalid [f5205, f6874, f6861]. When misses occur, exact binomial or another pre-declared interval is needed; the cited examples require about 474 trials with one allowed failure and 630 with two for a 1% miss-rate claim at 95% confidence, but provide no corresponding 99% counts [f14196, f6879, f6880]. False-alarm claims instead use exposure-based rates: zero events over T representative hours gives an approximately 3/T upper rate bound at 95% confidence, so 300 event-free hours supports fewer than one event per 100 hours [f5448, f6657, f224].
